verification.heading: Verification pass — September 25, 2026
verification.markdown:
Checked 2026-09-25 by verification agent G6 (sweep #2). **Job 1 was done by fetching primary hosts directly (legislature enacted-bill lists, the Revisor's section pages and history lines, the AG press-release index), not by web search.** The session's WebSearch budget was exhausted, so none of the SWEEP search strings were run.
- **2026 law-change sweep (primary-host fetch):** no 2025–26 change to any statute this file relies on.
  - **2026 session.** The Senate "Truly Agreed and Finally Passed" list for 2026 has 102 bills (https://www.senate.mo.gov/BillTracking/BillStatus/TATFP?year=2026&session=R). None concerns contractor licensing, building codes, CO or smoke alarms, seller-disclosure forms, home solicitation (§§ 407.700–.720), or chimneys and fireplaces. Two real-estate bills were truly agreed, SB 973 and HB 2636. Per the Senate TAFP summary report (https://www.senate.mo.gov/26info/TATFP2026Report.pdf) and the House bill summary (https://documents.house.mo.gov/billtracking/bills261/sumpdf/HB2636T.pdf), they add wholesaler disclosures (§ 407.3600), sale-leaseback rules (§ 442.920), mortgage modification (§§ 443.920–.925), and an insurance-policy anti-assignment rule (§ 379.135). None touches § 339.730, § 442.600, § 407.020/.025, or §§ 407.700–.720. Governor action on them was not confirmed. The Senate 2026 bill list (SB 834–1195) has no CO, smoke-alarm, contractor, building-code, or chimney title. The House bill list returned 403, so House-originated CO bills that did not pass were not screened.
  - **2025 session.** The TAFP list has 69 bills (https://www.senate.mo.gov/BillTracking/BillStatus/TATFP?year=2025&session=R). The only real-estate items are HB 595 and HB 596. Neither appears in the history of § 339.730, which still ends "A.L. 1998 H.B. 1601, eff. 1-01-99".
  - **Statute history lines re-read on revisor.mo.gov.** No 2025 or 2026 amendment appears in any of these:
    - § 407.700: L. 1973.
    - § 407.705: A.L. 1986 S.B. 685.
    - § 407.710: L. 1973.
    - § 407.020: last A.L. 2020 S.B. 591.
    - § 407.025: last A.L. 2020 S.B. 591.
    - § 339.730: 1998.
    - § 442.600: 1991.
    - § 64.170: last A.L. 2008 S.B. 1181.
  - **Revisor "Recent Sections" list** (https://revisor.mo.gov/main/recent.aspx): the 2025–26 changes it shows in chapters 64, 67 and 82 are farm-building fire codes, master plans, housing-code registration fees, construction-manager and design-build procurement, and nuisance/vacant-building procedure. None changes § 64.170 county code authority.
  - **CO law.** The DFS smoke/CO page still presents CO alarms as an NFPA "should" recommendation, with no 2025–26 law noted (https://dfs.dps.mo.gov/safetytips/smoke-carbon-monoxide-alarms.php). HB 2429 is confirmed as an introduced CO and smoke-detector bill (https://house.mo.gov/billtracking/bills101/bilsum/intro/sHB2429I.htm).
  - **AG news.** https://ago.mo.gov/press-releases/ shows 2025–26 contractor-fraud actions (titles only), none chimney-specific. Added to §8 without names.
  - **FTC rule.** 16 CFR 429.0 was re-read (eCFR current as of Sep 22, 2026). The $25 at-residence threshold and the buyer-initiated repair exclusion are unchanged.
- **Mirror spot-check:** n/a.
- **Dead links:**
  - **Resolve:** all revisor.mo.gov section URLs, dfs.dps.mo.gov, house.mo.gov HB 2429 summary, ecfr.gov, and stlouis-mo.gov/government/departments/license/. That St. Louis page still lists "Apply for a Construction - Contracting Business License".

sections.rawHeading: 1 · Licensing (GOV — high confidence on absence; local detail partial)
sections.title: State licensing and registration
sections.confidenceNote: high confidence on absence; local detail partial
sections.markdown:
**No statewide license or registration covers chimney work in Missouri.** Missouri has **no state general-contractor, residential-builder, or home-improvement license.** Chimney masonry, relining, and sweeping fall outside any state credential. Licensing is **LOCAL**, city by city:
- **Kansas City (KCMO)** issues contractor licenses through City Planning & Development. The categories include a **Residential Building Contractor** license, which "may construct, structurally alter, or enlarge any one or two family detached dwelling or townhouse," and a **Gas-Fired Appliance Contractor** license, which may "install, erect, alter, repair, service, and reset gas-fired appliances." Applicants obtain a Certificate of Qualification. They must be at least 21, hold a HS diploma or GED, and submit **examination results from a recognized agency (e.g., ICC or Prometric)**. **KCMO has no masonry, fireplace, or chimney license category** (KCMO contractor licensing page; bulletin "Contractor Licensing & Certification Requirements"). Lookup: city.kcmo.org/kc/Codes/LicensedContractors.
- **City of St. Louis:** the License Collector issues a **Construction – Contracting Business License**, which is separate from its general Graduated Business License. It is a business license, not a competency exam. *(Specific requirements not confirmed; see blockers.)*
- **Other cities** (e.g., Springfield, Columbia) may run their own regimes. *(Not verified in this pass.)*

"Licensed and bonded" in Missouri almost always means a city credential, valid only inside that jurisdiction.

sections.title: What the credential does not test
sections.markdown: Statewide, there is **nothing to verify for chimney work**: no exam, no registry, no bond requirement. Even where a city license exists, KC's is exam-based but tests general building knowledge through ICC/Prometric-type exams and has **no chimney or masonry class**. Individual certs (CSIA CCS, C-DET; NCSG CCP/CCR) and an independent audit fill a total vacuum here.

sections.rawHeading: 3 · Home sale (GOV — high confidence on absence; the notable finding)
sections.title: Seller disclosure when a home sells
sections.confidenceNote: high confidence on absence; the notable finding
sections.markdown:
**Missouri has NO statute requiring a seller-disclosure statement, and no chimney-specific disclosure statute.** The disclosure duties Missouri does have point elsewhere:
- **Common law:** sellers must not conceal or misrepresent known material defects.
- **Real-estate licensees, not sellers:** a licensee acting as the seller's agent "shall disclose to any customer all adverse material facts actually known or that should have been known by the licensee" (**RSMo § 339.730**). That duty contains no form requirement.
- **Stigma, not condition:** RSMo § 442.600 says psychological stigma (homicide, suicide, etc.) is *not* a material fact that must be disclosed. It says nothing about chimneys.

In practice many sales use a voluntary Missouri REALTORS® seller's disclosure form. Using it is contractual, not statutory, and a seller can decline it or sell "as is." *(The form's current number and chimney/fireplace wording were not verified in this pass; don't quote them.)* No inspection is mandated at transfer; NFPA 211 Level 2 stays a NATIONAL STANDARD. This is a **disclosure void**, not a mandate.

sections.rawHeading: 4 · Consumer remedies (GOV — high confidence; cancellation caveat corrected)
sections.title: Consumer remedies and cancellation rights
sections.markdown:
- **Missouri Merchandising Practices Act (MMPA).** **RSMo § 407.020** declares unlawful "any deception, fraud, false pretense, false promise, misrepresentation, unfair practice or the concealment, suppression, or omission of any material fact" in connection with a sale. The **AG's Consumer Protection Division** enforces it. **RSMo § 407.025** also gives consumers a **private right of action** for **actual damages**, with discretionary **punitive damages** and **attorney's fees**, and class actions are allowed. There is no automatic trebling. Since 2020 (SB 591), a plaintiff must show the conduct would mislead a **"reasonable consumer"** and prove damages "with a reasonable degree of certainty."
- **Home-solicitation cancellation — narrower than it looks.** **RSMo §§ 407.700–407.720** give a right to cancel "until midnight of the third business day after the day on which the buyer signs" (§ 407.705). But § 407.700 defines a home solicitation sale as a **"consumer credit sale"** solicited at the buyer's residence. **A cash or card door-knock chimney sale on the spot may not be covered by the Missouri statute.** For those sales, the **federal FTC Cooling-Off Rule (16 CFR Part 429, NATIONAL)** gives a 3-business-day cancellation right on door-to-door sales of **$25 or more** made at the buyer's home. That rule excludes repair or maintenance visits the buyer initiated, except for extra goods or services sold during the visit.

Complaints: ago.mo.gov consumer complaint portal.

sections.rawHeading: 5 · Permits & codes (GOV — high confidence on absence; genuine patchwork)
sections.title: Permits and building codes
sections.confidenceNote: high confidence on absence; genuine patchwork
sections.markdown:
**Missouri has no statewide residential building code.** Code adoption is local:
- **Cities** adopt codes under municipal and home-rule authority.
- **First- and second-classification counties** may adopt building regulations by order or ordinance (**RSMo § 64.170**). A county that had no code before Aug 28, 2001 needs **voter approval** to adopt one.
- **Unincorporated rural areas may have no code and no permit process at all.**

Kansas City and St. Louis each maintain their own IRC/IBC adoptions *(current editions not confirmed in this pass)*. Where a building department exists, chimney relines, rebuilds, crowns, and solid-fuel appliance installs are generally permit work; routine sweeps and like-for-like caps generally are not. This state needs the local-variance disclaimer heavily.

sections.title: Carbon monoxide and smoke alarm law
sections.markdown: **Missouri has NO statewide residential carbon-monoxide-alarm statute** found as of Sep 2026. The Missouri Division of Fire Safety's own smoke/CO page presents CO alarms only as an NFPA **recommendation**, not a state mandate. The CO bill cited earlier, **HB 2429**, was introduced in the **101st General Assembly (2022)** and not enacted. CO requirements are **LOCAL** only, through adopted building and fire codes. There is no pre-sale CO certificate. A permitted chimney or solid-fuel job is still the natural moment to add alarms.

sections.title: Solid fuel and environmental rules
sections.markdown: No statewide burn-ban or stove-emission regime. Not a material content section for MO.

sections.title: Scam patterns and enforcement
sections.markdown: The Missouri AG's Consumer Protection Division pursues home-repair contractors under the MMPA. The AG's press-release index (ago.mo.gov/press-releases, read Sep 25, 2026) shows repeated 2025–26 contractor-fraud actions — restitution judgments and felony charges against home-remodeling, roofing, and construction contractors, including one targeting tornado victims (May 2026). Only the titles were read, so do not name defendants or quote them. None is chimney-specific. The door-knock "we noticed your chimney" pitch is an MMPA misrepresentation scenario. Cancellation runs through § 407.705 if the sale is on credit, or through the FTC Cooling-Off Rule otherwise. **No MO chimney-sweep-specific enforcement action has been confirmed.** Use patterns, not names.

sections.title: Season calendar
sections.markdown: Continental climate, colder in the north, with hot humid summers. Burn season ~Oct–Mar. Rush: SEP–NOV. Best booking: APR–JUN.

sections.title: Price seeding (internal)
sections.markdown: The Kansas City and St. Louis metros run **near to slightly above national**; rural areas and the Ozarks run below national. Regionalize modestly upward for the two metros.

story.heading: The story
story.markdown:
Missouri is a **near-total regulatory vacuum on both axes**, and that is what makes it unusual. It has **no state chimney license, no statewide building code, no statewide CO statute, and no statute requiring a seller-disclosure form.** Even its door-to-door cancellation law covers only *credit* sales, so a cash door-knock scare sale leans on the federal FTC rule instead.

So Missouri **BREAKS the master finding's clean inverse.** The correlation predicts that no-license states deliver real mandatory disclosure to compensate, but Missouri gives neither. It is a rare double-weak state where the leverage lives almost entirely in the MMPA (§§ 407.020, 407.025, with punitive damages and fees available). The messages are blunt: **there is nothing to "look up" statewide, and no statute makes the seller hand you a disclosure form. Get your own inspection, and lean on the MMPA if you're defrauded.** That double vacuum is exactly the gap this site exists to fill.
